title: Cricket Australia widens Sandpapergate forum to 2017-18 Ashes
excerpt: The independent forum will now examine ball management across the whole 2017-18 season, as Usman Khawaja's memoir keeps the scandal alive.
content_html:
Cricket Australia has widened its independent forum into the 2018 ball-tampering scandal to include the home Ashes series that preceded it, as the fallout from Usman Khawaja's autobiography continues to divide the sport.

Terms of reference released on Friday show the forum, led by senior counsel Fiona McLeod, will examine ball-management practices in the Australian men's team across the whole 2017-18 season. That season included the 4-0 Ashes win over England, as well as all four Tests of the tour of South Africa, the events of 24 March 2018 in Cape Town, and how Cricket Australia's own investigation was run at the time.

What the forum will and won't do

Taking part is voluntary and the process is expected to run for six weeks. It will not hand out new sanctions or decide who was individually responsible. What players and staff say will stay confidential, but a report on the main themes and recommendations will go to the board and is to be made public.

Interim chair David Boon said: "This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard."

The board first announced the forum on 18 November in Hobart, when Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg ruled out reopening the original investigation.

How the scandal was reopened

The saga resurfaced in early November with Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr. The former opener, who retired this year after 88 Tests, claims the whole squad knew about the plan to use sandpaper in Cape Town, and that the tactic had already been tried in the previous Test in Port Elizabeth. He has also said Cricket Australia's investigators never interviewed him.

Cameron Bancroft, who was caught on camera with the sandpaper, backed that account in a column for The West Australian on 18 November and admitted he had held back details from the 2018 inquiry. David Warner has also supported Khawaja and called for an open, public inquiry.

Others strongly dispute the claims. Test captain Pat Cummins described them as "utter nonsense" and has said he did not know sandpaper was being used. Mitchell Starc has also rejected them, and the four bowlers who played in Cape Town issued a joint denial in 2021.

Cricket Australia's original inquiry found only Steve Smith, Warner and Bancroft knew of the plan. Smith and Warner were banned for 12 months and Bancroft for nine. Smith has not commented since the book was released.
